verdict.reasoning: A fault class must be inferred from what a service is doing wrong, and here no service produced a signal of doing anything. The change records are the strongest evidence and they point away from every change-driven class: all entries are first creations by platform-automation with no prior version, so there is no artifact to have regressed (bad_deploy), no value edited away from a working one (bad_config), and nothing to roll back [tr_08bfa0bd702e, tr_88ef5ea29f07]. The hang-versus-silence discriminators cannot be applied: process_freeze and network_partition are told apart by whether the culprit logs that it cannot reach anything, and no logs exist for either service queried [tr_38611975bcd5, tr_f5e3ed08eb82]. Nothing in the board shows a no-space-left message, a decode failure, or a saturation signal, so disk_fill, datastore_corruption and resource_exhaustion have no positive support either. The nginx error ratio is explicitly non-sustained with an absent baseline, so it cannot anchor a regression [tr_0b7d99223f50], and the total absence of traces rules out attributing the fault to any named downstream call [tr_ebf55ae35440]. The coincidence of first-creation timestamps three minutes before onset across two independent services is the one coherent pattern, and it is consistent with an environment mid-bring-up rather than a steady-state failure.
verdict.root_cause: The evidence does not establish a failing mechanism. Nearly every dispatch returned an empty answer: no nginx logs [tr_38611975bcd5], no compose-post logs [tr_f5e3ed08eb82], no nginx traces across a full hour [tr_ebf55ae35440], and no span-metric samples at all for compose-post, home-timeline or user-timeline in either the incident or baseline window [tr_0d99b3b3f553, tr_6a0a1142c89c, tr_73654c07a93e]. The most defensible reading is that this environment was being brought up from scratch at 16:03 and alerted at 16:06 before the stack had stabilised or begun emitting telemetry; the specialists found no running-state fault to attribute. Naming a culprit service and mechanism on this board would be invention.

draft.title: Critical alert at the edge with a near-silent telemetry board

sections.body: The page named nginx-web-server, severity critical, with a declared blast radius of four services: the nginx front end plus compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service. Triage crossed three edges that were never themselves measured, so the downstream list should be read as an assumption about topology, not as an observation. Nothing on the board reproduces the condition that fired the alert. That is the single most important thing to carry forward: by the time anyone looked, there was no alertable signal left to inspect, and no record of which series the alert evaluated.
sections.heading: What the responder saw first

sections.body: The only metric that returned anything at all was the span-status error ratio for nginx-web-server over the half hour ending at the alert. Five samples, mean around 1%, a single peak just under 5%, and the comparison tool reported no sustained departure. Three of the five samples had no defined value, which the tool reads as intervals with no traffic through the front end at all. So the shape is not a wave of errors; it is a trickle of requests with essentially one interval carrying the elevated ratio. Crucially, the preceding thirty minutes produced zero samples, so there is no before to compare the after against. A responder reading the chart alone could easily mistake "rose from nothing" for "regressed from healthy." It did not; the baseline is absent, not flat.
sections.heading: The one signal that was not empty

sections.body: Loki returned no lines for the nginx front-end pods across the window spanning onset, and no lines for compose-post-service across a full hour. The query was not severity-filtered in either case, so the silence covers ordinary access and startup output too, not just errors. Tempo returned no traces whatsoever for nginx-web-server over an hour. Span-metric error ratios for compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service were empty in the incident window and equally empty in the baseline window. Two of these results carried truncation flags despite being empty, which is an awkward combination and means the emptiness deserved one confirming query with a broader selector before being treated as fact. Nobody ran it.
sections.heading: Everything else came back empty

sections.body: A twenty-four hour lookback on nginx-web-server contains exactly three entries, and all three land in a roughly two-second span about three minutes before onset (T-3m). They are creations, not edits: a Service and a ConfigMap named for nginx-thrift, then first creation of the workload container. compose-post-service shows the identical pattern — Service and ConfigMap in the same second, container one second later, also around T-3m, also first creation. Every entry on both services is attributed to platform-automation; no human actor appears anywhere in the window. This is the signature of an environment being stood up from nothing, not of a change to something that was already serving.
sections.heading: The change record, which is where the story actually turns

sections.body: Several plausible stories were killed and should not be re-walked. A configuration edit regressing nginx: there are no prior versions of those objects in twenty-four hours, so there is nothing to have been edited away from. A version or image bump: no version-change event of any kind is recorded. A rollback as remediation: there is no previous revision of either workload to roll back to. Drift from a change made hours earlier: the log is empty until the final three minutes. An ad-hoc human action: the actor column is uniformly automation. On the telemetry side, a crash loop at compose-post-service would have left startup and termination banners; readiness churn would have left probe lines; a hanging downstream call would normally leave unterminated spans at the front end. None of those signatures are present. Equally, the absence of downstream span metrics cannot be read as those services going quiet at onset, because the pre-incident window is just as empty — the gap predates the event.
sections.heading: Dead ends worth keeping

sections.body: The evidence does not establish a failing mechanism, and naming a culprit service here would be invention. The most defensible reading is that this environment was being brought up from scratch at roughly T-3m and alerted at T+0 before the stack had stabilised or started emitting telemetry. The specialists found no running-state failure to attribute. Confidence is low and no fix class applies. Treat the empty results as unresolved ambiguity rather than as negative findings: an empty answer is not a clean bill of health, and at least two of them were flagged truncated.
sections.heading: What this record concludes, and what it refuses to conclude

sections.body: Query the orchestrator. No dispatch ever asked whether the newly created workloads reached Running and Ready, or whether they were stuck pulling images, pending scheduling, or restarting before a first log line existed. That gap alone could explain every empty panel on this board. Second, confirm the Loki and Tempo emptiness with broader selectors — drop the pod-name regex and query by namespace, since a label or naming mismatch would present identically to genuine silence. Third, note that only the error-ratio template was ever run; latency and saturation were never measured for any of the four services, so a slow-dependency or resource-pressure mechanism remains entirely untested. Fourth, establish which signal the critical alert actually evaluated. Finally, the three unmeasured edges crossed during triage may conceal a backend — post storage, a cache or document store, or a service-discovery layer — that no specialist was ever dispatched against.
sections.heading: What the next responder should do first

proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that the environment stays broken while nobody acts, and the alert from 16:06:34 continues unaddressed. The risk of the alternative - acting anyway - is larger and concrete: rollback_image and revert_config both require a prior image tag or prior configuration, and the change history records only first creations for both nginx-web-server [tr_08bfa0bd702e] and compose-post-service [tr_88ef5ea29f07], so there is no prior state to return to and either action would fail or deploy an arbitrary tag. restart_service requires evidence pointing at process state; with zero logs, zero traces and zero span metrics [tr_f5e3ed08eb82, tr_ebf55ae35440, tr_0d99b3b3f553] there is no such evidence, and recreating a container three minutes into a cold bring-up would reset whatever startup progress exists and destroy the very first log lines a diagnosis depends on.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if the stack is in fact wedged in a state a container recreate would clear - for example if the orchestrator shows compose-post-service or nginx-web-server stuck in CrashLoopBackOff or started before a dependency was listening. Nothing on this board shows that: the logs that would carry a crash banner are empty [tr_f5e3ed08eb82], and the only non-empty metric is a non-sustained, baseline-less nginx error ratio [tr_0b7d99223f50]. If a pod-state query returns a restart count climbing or a container in a terminal error state, restart_service on that service becomes defensible and this abstention should be revisited immediately.
proposal.blast_radius: None from this proposal, since nothing is changed. For context on what was declined: a restart or redeploy of nginx-web-server would be seen by every external caller of the edge and by its three downstreams compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service; a restart of compose-post-service would be seen by nginx-web-server as reset inbound connections. Both would also disturb the as-yet-unmeasured bring-up sequence for the whole social-network namespace.
proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no change in any observable signal should follow from this proposal. The correct next step is observation, not remediation: query the orchestrator for pod/container state (Running, Ready, ImagePullBackOff, Pending, CrashLoopBackOff) for nginx-thrift and compose-post-service around 16:03:32-16:06:40, and re-run the Loki and Tempo queries with a broader selector (namespace only, no pod regex) to separate a genuinely silent stack from a label/selector mismatch. Either of those would produce the first positive signal this board lacks.
